analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to address combined pollution risks and boost enforcement in overburdened communities.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to two House committees in April 2021 and died at the end of the 117th Congress without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Environmental Protection Agency to develop a protocol for evaluating the combined health effects of multiple pollution sources—air, water, chemicals, waste, and climate impacts—together, instead of one at a time. It would also require EPA to identify at least 100 communities that are disproportionately communities of color, low-income, or Tribal and that suffer more environmental law violations than average, analyze why the violations happen, and fix them within two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of overburdened communities—disproportionately people of color, low-income households, and Tribal communities—that currently absorb pollution from multiple sources and see more environmental violations than the national average. The bill would require EPA to assess their combined health risks and take concrete steps to cut violations in at least 100 of these communities, with public hearings designed to maximize resident input.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to publish a protocol within 180 days, finalize it within a year, and implement it within three years for assessing cumulative public health risks from multiple stressors, including pollution regulated under the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Safe Drinking Water Act, and toxic waste laws, plus climate impacts like extreme heat, flooding, wildfire smoke, and disease spread [S3].

Requires EPA to identify at least 100 environmental justice communities with above-average environmental law violations, engage with residents to find root causes, and implement measures within two years to bring violations significantly below the national average [S3].

Mandates at least four public hearings on the cumulative-risk protocol, held at times and locations meant to maximize input from affected residents, and public comment before the protocol is finalized [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Facilities that pollute—industrial plants, waste handlers, and other regulated sources—would face a regulatory process that counts their combined impact rather than each permit in isolation, and stronger enforcement attention in the 100 identified communities. State and local co-regulator agencies would share the work of reducing violations.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets firm deadlines and mandates but provides no new funding, so EPA would have to absorb the analysis, hearings, community engagement, and enforcement work within its existing budget, which could stretch or delay implementation [S3].

The cumulative-risk protocol could make it harder for any single facility to get a permit in an already overburdened area, a cost regulated industries and some state agencies would bear, and the bill leaves the definition of 'significantly below the national average' to EPA's discretion rather than fixing a number [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of communities that bear the brunt of stacked pollution and repeat violations, the bill offers a concrete process—measurement, hearings, and mandatory corrective action—without new spending. The costs fall mainly on regulated facilities facing a stricter permitting and enforcement lens and on agencies working within existing budgets. The main weakness is that deadlines without funding often slip in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Natural Resources committees and then to an Energy and Commerce subcommittee, where it sat with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on April 8, 2021, with no cosponsors [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Natural Resources Committee for consideration of the provisions in each committee's jurisdiction [S5].
Five days later it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The bill's action history shows no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and no cosponsors before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that discharge pollution into overburdened communities are better off: the bill that would have increased scrutiny of their combined impacts and required enforcement fixes in at least 100 such communities died without ever being considered, costing them nothing.

for.name: Rep. Diana DeGette
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing EPA to assess cumulative pollution risks and fix enforcement gaps in overburdened communities.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 8, 2021, sent it to its Environment and Climate Change subcommittee, and never held a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 8, 2021, and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors of either party and no votes or hearings, the record shows no organized support or opposition—only inaction in committee.

industries.industry: Industrial polluters (chemical plants, refineries, waste and disposal facilities)
industries.note: A cumulative-impact protocol would count these facilities' combined pollution burden when EPA evaluates risks and permits, and targeted enforcement in 100 overburdened communities would raise scrutiny of repeat violators. Their interest in the status quo ran against the health of residents in those communities.

The bill makes state and local co-regulators partners in identifying violation causes and cutting violations, adding coordination duties but also focusing enforcement resources where problems are worst.
